title: Race and ethnicity in the NBA
summary: This document covers the topic of race and ethnicity in the National Basketball Association (NBA), tracing its evolution throughout the league's history. It begins with current demographic statistics showing the league's composition (70.4% black, 17.5% white, 2.2% Latino, and 0.2% Asian players in 2023), noting the NBA has the highest percentage of black players among major North American professional sports leagues. The document then presents a historical timeline of racial milestones for players, including Wat Misaka as the first non-white and Asian American player (1947), the pioneering African American players of 1950 (Chuck Cooper, Harold Hunter, Nathaniel "Sweetwater" Clifton, Earl Lloyd, and Hank DeZonie), Don Barksdale as the first black All-Star (1953), unofficial racial quotas in the 1960s, and later firsts including Latino player Butch Lee (1978), Chinese player Wang Zhizhi (2001), and Jeremy Lin (2010). It also addresses the declining number of white American players in recent decades. Additional sections examine the history of coaches, highlighting Bill Russell as the first black head coach (1966) and subsequent coaching demographics; the emergence of non-white majority owners, beginning with Robert Johnson (2004) and including Michael Jordan, Vivek Ranadivé, and Joseph Tsai; and viewership demographics showing the NBA's uniquely diverse audience with the highest share of black viewers among major North American sports. The document concludes with discussion of the NBA's branding efforts, particularly the 2005 dress code and 2007 "Where Amazing Happens" campaign, which critics argue portrayed the league as "raceless" despite existing racial issues, followed by related articles, references, and further reading suggestions on topics like racial quotas and black participation in basketball.
